question: We're building a system that a city education office will use to assign children to primary schools, based on their home address and whether a sibling already attends the school. It doesn't accept or reject anyone; it only decides which school each child goes to. Is that the kind of system the AI Act lists with admission tools?
gold_answer: Annex III, point 3(a), lists AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels, so the point covers assigning persons to institutions, not only admitting or rejecting them. Under Article 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered to be high-risk. The answer explains what the point lists and does not decide whether the user's system is high-risk.

question: We sell our applicant-ranking tool to universities as advice for their admission committees, but we know some of them may simply reject everyone in the bottom half of the list. Does our risk management have to take that kind of use into account?
gold_source: Article 9(2), introductory text and point (b); Article 3, point (13)
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 9(2) makes the risk management system a continuous iterative process run throughout its entire lifecycle. Under point (b), it comprises the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse. Article 3, point (13), defines reasonably foreseeable misuse as the use of an AI system in a way that is not in accordance with its intended purpose, but which may result from reasonably foreseeable human behaviour or interaction with other systems, including other AI systems. If rejecting applicants on the basis of the list is such a use, its risks are evaluated under Article 9(2), point (b). The answer explains the definition and does not determine whether this particular use meets it, or whether the tool is high-risk.

question: Before we start selling our admission scoring system to universities, when does its technical documentation have to be ready, and can we leave it as it is after launch?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 11(1) requires the technical documentation to be drawn up before the system is placed on the market or put into service and to be kept up to date, so it is not left as it is after launch. The documentation is drawn up to demonstrate that the system complies with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2. The answer does not decide whether the system is high-risk.

question: I'm on the legal team. Our admission portal has a chat assistant that answers applicants' questions. Since when does the AI Act require that applicants are told they are talking to an AI, and is there a case where this is not needed?
gold_answer: Article 50(1) requires providers to ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. Article 50 is in Chapter IV, which is not among the exceptions in Article 113, third paragraph, so under the consolidated text of 27/07/2026 it applies from the general date in Article 113, second paragraph: 2 August 2026.

question: Our admission model is trained on past applicant data. Which fairness metric, for example demographic parity, does the AI Act require for it, and how big may the gap in admission rates between groups of applicants be?
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: abstain. The answer says in one sentence that the provisions name no fairness metric and no maximum gap between groups, and gives no metric or number. Background: under Article 10(1), high-risk AI systems which make use of techniques involving the training of AI models with data are developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet the quality criteria of Article 10(2) to (4); Article 10(2), points (f) and (g), require the data governance and management practices for the training, validation and testing data sets to concern the examination in view of possible biases and appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate possible biases identified; Article 10(3) requires the data sets to have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used.
